study.title: Isaiah 3 - Judgment on leadership, pride, and desolation of Zion
study.overview: Isaiah 3 describes the Lord's withdrawal from the basic support of the social and religious life of Jerusalem and Judah, followed by disorder, oppression, judgment against leaders, and humiliation of the daughters of Zion. The chapter shows that the national fall is not mere political accident: it is linked to public sin, arrogance and abuse of power. At the same time, the text preserves a clear moral distinction: the righteous will receive good, and the wicked will reap what he has done. The closure, with the groaning doors and the city sitting on the ground, summarizes the shame and mourning that accompany the ruin.

outline.title: The Lord removes the sustains from society
outline.explanation: The text announces the withdrawal of food, water and all forms of leadership - military, civil, judicial, religious and even human council leadership. The image is of total collapse: when God takes away the means of sustenance and government, human stability disappears. The commentators highlight that this includes both everyday life and public order.

outline.title: Immaturity in government and social conflict
outline.explanation: Boys and young people take over, while the people enter into oppression and disorder. No one wants to accept responsibility, because ruin is so deep that governing becomes impossible. The cause presented by the prophet is moral: Jerusalem stumbles because his words and works rise against the Lord, and the open behavior of the people remembers Sodom.

outline.title: God's moral justice against sin and against exploitative leaders
outline.explanation: The chapter distinguishes the righteous from the wicked: good will fall upon those who live correctly, and evil upon whomever practices evil. Then the Lord comes into court against the elders and leaders, accusing them of exploiting the vineyard and crushing the poor. The focus is not only on the weakness of the people, but the aggravated responsibility of those who should conduct justice.

outline.title: Pride of Zion's daughters and final humiliation
outline.explanation: The latter part denounces the vanity, seduction and luxury exhibited by the women of Zion. The Lord reverses the adornments in signs of shame: perfume turns a bad smell, beauty becomes a mark of mourning, and men fall by the sword. The end, with the doors crying and the city sitting on the floor, gives poetic form to complete devastation.

study.context: The notes link the chapter to calamities that would come upon Judah and Jerusalem, especially the Babylonian invasion and captivity. Matthew Henry also notes that the picture includes the desolation of the city and, in his reading, points to later stages of the national judgment. The common point of the commentators is that the chapter interprets the historical crisis as a divine judgment on public sin, corrupted leadership and pride.
study.theology: Isaiah 3 teaches that God governs not only individuals, but also social structures. When leadership corrupts, society suffers; when the people reject the Lord, the order created by Him breaks down in confusion. The chapter also affirms differentiated moral responsibility: the righteous is not forgotten, and the wicked will not escape the principle of retribution. There is also a theology of reversal: what seemed shine, strength and security - adornments, status, power, beauty - can be withdrawn in an instant, revealing human fragility. Finally, the text shows that the Lord also judges abuse against the poor, making it clear that social exploitation is spiritual offense.

scholarViews.insight: The withdrawal of all kinds of leadership would produce chaos and hunger, turning Judah and Jerusalem into a social desert.
The chapter announces the desolation of Judah and Jerusalem because of the sins of the people, including the withdrawal of the support of life and government.
The expression of "garothos" as princes is understood as fulfillment in the succession of weak and evil rulers until the fall of the city.

questions: What support of life and faith tends to treat as safer than the Lord Himself?
In what areas do our words and deeds show resistance to God, as in Isaiah 3:8-9?
How do we use authority, influence, or resources: to serve the vulnerable or to crush them?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to personal and community repentance. Examine whether you depend more on structures, appearance, and power than on obedience to the Lord. Reject any form of exhibitionist pride, especially when it hides spiritual emptiness. And if you exercise some leadership - in the house, in the church, in the work - remember that God charges justice, care and integrity, especially in relation to the weak.
study.uncertainty: The notes agree on the divine judgment on Jerusalem and Judah, but differ in the final historical reach: Matthew Henry also mentions the ruin completed by the Romans, while the other notes emphasize mainly Babylonian invasion and captivity. The chapter, in the given notes, does not solve all the details of this historical application alone.
